public_rationale: He predicted Cursor would not 'actually sell' for '$10 billion plus' and would instead get a lowball, pawn-shop-style deal that paid the CEO while staff made nothing. In June 2026 SpaceX formally agreed to buy the whole company for $60 billion in stock (e1). CNBC reports the acquisition closed on Aug. 14, 2026, citing filings (e2). Coverage of the closing filing says employee RSUs and options were converted into SpaceX equity or assumed by SpaceX (e3), so staff did not get nothing. This is the real $10B+ sale he set as the opposite of his forecast.
limitations: Closing terms come from news reports of the 8-K, not the filing itself, which could not be read.
The deal was paid in stock, so value realized by holders depends on SpaceX's share price and any lockups.
Some may argue that a sale to a company tied to the acquirer's own AI ambitions was unusual. It was still a full acquisition far above $10B.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Cursor will end in a poor deal that enriches its CEO while staff get nothing, rather than a healthy $10B+ sale.

statement.excerpt: In reality, I expect a Chumlee-esque deal that helps CEO Michael Truell buy a porsche while his staff makes nothing.

from_speaker: contrasted with Cursor selling "for a healthy amount — I'm talking $10 billion plus, and I mean actually sell"
not "the founders are hired in a strange contractual agreement that pays out investors and its assets are sold to Rick from Pawn Stars"
"helps CEO Michael Truell buy a porsche while his staff makes nothing"
our_interpretation: His own contrast sets the test. He predicts Cursor's exit will be a lowball, pawn-shop-style deal, such as an acqui-hire or licensing deal or a sale well under $10 billion, that pays the CEO and investors but leaves staff with little. He sets this against a real sale of the company for $10 billion or more.
No deadline is given, so the forecast is open-ended. It can be settled early by Cursor's actual exit event.
The central test is the deal's form and size, a real acquisition at $10B+ versus a Chumlee-style deal. How staff are treated is a secondary part of the same prediction.
criteria.support_condition: Cursor's exit is an acqui-hire, a licensing-plus-hiring deal, a fire sale, or a sale well under $10 billion, in which the founders or CEO are paid and most staff get little or nothing.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Cursor is actually acquired outright (the whole company, not just its founders) at $10 billion or more, and staff equity is honored in the deal.

evidence.excerpt: SpaceX on Tuesday announced it entered a formal agreement to buy the artificial intelligence startup Cursor for $60 billion worth of stock
evidence.explanation: A formal agreement to buy the whole company for $60 billion in stock, six times his $10B 'healthy amount' bar. It is a full purchase, not a licensing or acqui-hire deal.

evidence.excerpt: SpaceX completed its $60 billion acquisition of Cursor on Aug. 14, according to financial filings.
evidence.explanation: The sale closed. Cursor 'actually sold' for well over $10 billion, which is the outcome his forecast said would not happen.

evidence.excerpt: Vested Cursor RSUs convert into another 1,752,426 Class A shares, before tax withholding. Then SpaceX assumes unvested RSUs and options as about 29.1 million new SpaceX RSUs and 44.4 million SpaceX options.
evidence.locator: section 'What the SpaceX Cursor deal paid', paragraph 2
evidence.explanation: Reports the closing 8-K: employee RSUs and options were converted into SpaceX equity or assumed by SpaceX. That cuts against 'his staff makes nothing.' This is a smaller outlet summarizing the filing.

evidence.excerpt: Cursor was on track to close a $2 billion funding round from the likes of Andreessen Horowitz, Thrive, and Nvidia that would have valued the AI coding startup at $50 billion
evidence.explanation: Shows the $60B price was above Cursor's last private valuation talks, not a distressed sale.

conclusive_event.meets_rule: Cursor completed an outright acquisition of the whole company at $60 billion, above the $10B bar, with staff equity converted or assumed. Under the early-resolution rule this contradicts the forecast.
